pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.before:
(c) (absorption mirror) let $g\in\mathfrak h$ be a unit vector, let
$\Psi_{1}^{g}(t)$ denote the first interaction-picture Dyson term of the model
with initial vector $\Phi_{0}:=v_{b}\otimes g$, and define
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t):=\bigl\langle v_{b}\otimes g,\Psi_{1}(t)\bigr\rangle, \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t):=\bigl\langle v_{a}\otimes\Omega,\Psi_{1}^{g}(t)\bigr\rangle .$$
Then for every $t\ge0$
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t)=-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{t} e^{-i\Delta s/\hbar}\,\overline{\bigl\langle M,\,e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g\bigr\rangle_{\mathfrak h}}\,ds, \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)=-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{t} e^{+i\Delta s/\hbar}\,\overline{\bigl\langle M,\,e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g\bigr\rangle_{\mathfrak h}}\,ds,$$
so that $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)$ is obtained from
$\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t)$ by the replacement $\Delta\mapsto-\Delta$; in
particular $|\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)|$ at detuning $\Delta$ equals
$|\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t)|$ at detuning $-\Delta$ for the same unit vector $g$;
pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.after:
(c) (absorption mirror) let $g\in\mathfrak h$ be a unit vector, let
$\Psi_1^g(t)$ be the first interaction-picture Dyson term with initial
vector $\Phi_0=v_b\otimes g$, defined as a norm integral using the
finite-photon-sector creation/contraction action, and define the physical
transition amplitudes with the output vector in the first slot,
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t):=\langle\Psi_1(t),v_b\otimes g\rangle,\qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t):=\langle\Psi_1^g(t),v_a\otimes\Omega\rangle.$$
Then for every $t\ge0$,
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t)=-\frac{i\eta_0}{\hbar}\int_0^te^{-i\Delta s/\hbar}\langle M,e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g\rangle_{\mathfrak h}\,ds,\qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)=-\frac{i\eta_0}{\hbar}\int_0^te^{+i\Delta s/\hbar}\overline{\langle M,e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g\rangle_{\mathfrak h}}\,ds,$$
and hence
$$\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)=-\overline{\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t)},\qquad |\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)|=|\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}(t)|.$$
This compares the reverse transitions for the same level pair, the same
unit one-photon vector $g$ and the same real coupling $\eta_0$, retaining
arbitrary complex Hermitian dipole matrices and transverse mode vectors;

pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.before: 1.1 [The first Dyson term in the one-photon sector at level $b$] By [F1] and [F2], $\Psi_{1}(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{t}V(s)\Psi_{0}\,ds$ with $V(s)=e^{isH_{0}/\hbar}Be^{-isH_{0}/\hbar}$, and by [F3] $e^{-isH_{0}/\hbar}\Psi_{0}=e^{-isE_{a}/\hbar}\Psi_{0}$ while $B\Psi_{0}=\eta_{0}\sum_{j}D^{W}_{j}v_{a}\otimes g_{j}$ by [F1]. Hence $V(s)\Psi_{0}=\eta_{0}e^{-isE_{a}/\hbar}\sum_{j}e^{isH_{0}/\hbar}(D^{W}_{j}v_{a}\otimes g_{j})$, and pairing with $v_{b}\otimes f$, $f\in\mathfrak h$, gives by [F3] and [F4] $$\bigl\langle v_{b}\otimes f,V(s)\Psi_{0}\bigr\rangle=\eta_{0}e^{-is\Delta/\hbar}\sum_{j}c_{j}\bigl\langle f,e^{is\varepsilon/\hbar}g_{j}\bigr\rangle_{\mathfrak h}=\eta_{0}e^{-is\Delta/\hbar}\bigl\langle f,e^{is\varepsilon/\hbar}M\bigr\rangle_{\mathfrak h},$$ because the pairing is conjugate-linear in the first argument and $M=\sum_{j}c_{j}g_{j}$. Therefore $$\bigl\langle v_{b}\otimes f,\Psi_{1}(t)\bigr\rangle=-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-is\Delta/\hbar}\bigl\langle f,e^{is\varepsilon/\hbar}M\bigr\rangle_{\mathfrak h}ds=\bigl\langle f,A_{b}(\cdot,t)\bigr\rangle_{\mathfrak h},$$ the last identity being the definition of $A_{b}(\cdot,t)$ in clause (d) of the model's spectral-transition reading with $t$ in place of $s$; since $f\in\mathfrak h$ was arbitrary, the component in question is $v_{b}\otimes A_{b}(\cdot,t)$. [F1, F3, F4, F7, algebra, F2]
pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.after: 1.1 [The first Dyson term in the one-photon sector at level $b$] By [F1] and [F2], $\Psi_1(t)=-(i/\hbar)\int_0^tV(s)\Psi_0\,ds$ with $V(s)=e^{isH_0/\hbar}Be^{-isH_0/\hbar}$. The free initial phase is $e^{-isH_0/\hbar}\Psi_0=e^{-isE_a/\hbar}\Psi_0$, and $B\Psi_0=\eta_0\sum_jD_j^Wv_a\otimes g_j$. In the linear-first convention, the coefficient of $v_b$ in $e^{isH_a/\hbar}D_j^Wv_a$ is $\langle e^{isH_a/\hbar}D_j^Wv_a,v_b\rangle=e^{isE_b/\hbar}c_j$ by [F3]. Consequently $Q_bV(s)\Psi_0=v_b\otimes\eta_0 e^{-is\Delta/\hbar}e^{is\varepsilon/\hbar}M$. The bounded projection passes through the vector integral, giving $Q_b\Psi_1(t)=v_b\otimes[-(i\eta_0/\hbar)\int_0^te^{-is\Delta/\hbar}e^{is\varepsilon/\hbar}M\,ds]=v_b\otimes A_b(\cdot,t)$ by the definition of $A_b$. Equivalently, for every $f\in\mathfrak h$, $\langle\Psi_1(t),v_b\otimes f\rangle=\langle A_b(\cdot,t),f\rangle$, with all coefficients in the linear first slot. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, algebra]

pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.before: 2.2 [Absorption mirror] With $\Phi_{0}=v_{b}\otimes g$, unit $g\in\mathfrak h$, the same computation as in step 1.1 with [F1] gives $B\Phi_{0}=\eta_{0}\sum_{j}D^{W}_{j}v_{b}\otimes\phi(g_{j})g$; pairing the vacuum component $\Omega$ of $\phi(g_{j})g=A_{+}(g_{j})g+A_{-}(g_{j})g$ and using $A_{-}(g_{j})g=\langle g,g_{j}\rangle_{\mathfrak h}\Omega$ ([F1]) yields $$V(s)\Phi_{0}=\eta_{0}e^{-isE_{b}/\hbar}\sum_{j}e^{isH_{0}/\hbar}\bigl(D^{W}_{j}v_{b}\otimes\langle e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g,g_{j}\rangle_{\mathfrak h}\Omega\bigr)+\text{(two-photon terms)},$$ whose inner product with $v_{a}\otimes\Omega$ is $\eta_{0}e^{is\Delta/\hbar}\sum_{j}\overline{c_{j}}\langle e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g,g_{j}\rangle_{\mathfrak h}=\eta_{0}e^{is\Delta/\hbar}\overline{\langle M,e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g\rangle}_{\mathfrak h}$ by [F3] and the identity $\overline{\langle M,h\rangle}_{\mathfrak h}=\sum_{j}c_{j}\overline{\langle g_{j},h\rangle}_{\mathfrak h}=\sum_{j}\overline{c_{j}}\langle h,g_{j}\rangle_{\mathfrak h}$. Integrating against $-\frac{i}{\hbar}$ gives the displayed $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}$; step 1.1 with the same $g$ in place of $f$ gives $\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}$. The two integrands differ exactly by $e^{\mp i\Delta s/\hbar}$, which is the replacement $\Delta\mapsto-\Delta$. This proves (c). [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, algebra]
pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.after: 2.2 [Absorption mirror] For a unit $g\in\mathfrak h$, the first Dyson term with initial vector $\Phi_0=v_b\otimes g$ is well defined as a norm integral: the free evolution preserves the one-photon sector, and the creation/contraction bounds [F1] bound each vertex uniformly from that sector to the vacuum plus two-photon sectors. The sector maps are bounded and free evolution is strongly continuous, giving a norm-continuous integrand; these sector formulas supply the extension even when $g\notin D(\varepsilon)$. No full Dyson-series assertion for this initial vector is used. Set $h_s=e^{-is\varepsilon/\hbar}g$. The vacuum component of $\phi(g_j)h_s$ is $\langle h_s,g_j\rangle\Omega$ in the linear-first convention. The coefficient of $v_a$ in $e^{isH_a/\hbar}D_j^Wv_b$ is $e^{isE_a/\hbar}\overline{c_j}$ by [F3]; thus $\langle V(s)\Phi_0,v_a\otimes\Omega\rangle=\eta_0e^{is\Delta/\hbar}\sum_j\overline{c_j}\langle h_s,g_j\rangle=\eta_0e^{is\Delta/\hbar}\overline{\langle M,h_s\rangle}$. Integrating with $-i/\hbar$ in the first slot gives the displayed absorption amplitude. Step 1.1 and unitarity give $\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}=-(i\eta_0/\hbar)\int_0^te^{-is\Delta/\hbar}\langle e^{is\varepsilon/\hbar}M,g\rangle ds=-(i\eta_0/\hbar)\int_0^te^{-is\Delta/\hbar}\langle M,h_s\rangle ds$. Since $\eta_0$ is real, conjugating this scalar integral proves $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}=-\overline{\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}}$ and equal moduli, including $t=0$ or $\eta_0=0$. This proves (c) for the full complex couplings. [F1, F3, F4, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.before: - **The mirror is an algebraic identity, not a detailed-balance theorem.** Clause (c) relates two first-order amplitudes of the same model that differ by the sign of the detuning; it assumes nothing about populations, temperatures or equilibrium. The equal-modulus statement is a statement about $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}$ on opposite detunings.
pthm-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-emiss.after: - **The mirror is an algebraic identity, not a detailed-balance theorem.** Clause (c) relates the reverse first-order amplitudes of the same level pair and the same one-photon vector by $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}=-\overline{\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}}$. It assumes nothing about populations, temperatures or equilibrium; equality of moduli follows from the Hermitian coupling and the linear-first amplitude convention.

(c) (equal stimulated coefficients) for the two-level case $d=2$ with
orthonormal eigenvectors $v_{\uparrow},v_{\downarrow}$, $H_av_{\uparrow}
=E_{\uparrow}v_{\uparrow}$, $H_av_{\downarrow}=E_{\downarrow}v_{\downarrow}$
and $\Delta=E_{\uparrow}-E_{\downarrow}>0$, the actual upward and downward
first-order amplitudes under the same real prescribed field obey
$$A^{(1)}_{\downarrow\uparrow}(t,s)=-\overline{A^{(1)}_{\uparrow\downarrow}(t,s)}.$$
In particular their squared moduli, the model's first-order stimulated
emission and absorption coefficients, are equal. For the monochromatic
field of (b), the upward co-rotating component at detuning
$\Delta-\hbar\omega$ and the reverse downward component at the opposite

transition conjugates its matrix element and swaps the two exponential
components, with the same overall minus-conjugation relation;

pthm-nrqm-light-matter-stimulated-dipole.after: 2.1 [Equal stimulated coefficients] Let $w(r):=\langle V(r)v_{\downarrow},v_{\uparrow}\rangle$. The real prescribed field and Hermitian $D_j^W$ make $V(r)$ Hermitian, so [F2] gives $\langle V(r)v_{\uparrow},v_{\downarrow}\rangle=\overline{w(r)}$. Step 1.1 gives $A^{(1)}_{\uparrow\downarrow}=-(i/\hbar)\int_s^te^{i\Delta(r-s)/\hbar}w(r)dr$ and $A^{(1)}_{\downarrow\uparrow}=-(i/\hbar)\int_s^te^{-i\Delta(r-s)/\hbar}\overline{w(r)}dr=-\overline{A^{(1)}_{\uparrow\downarrow}}$, proving equal squared moduli for arbitrary complex Hermitian couplings. In the monochromatic decomposition of step 1.2, conjugation exchanges the positive and negative drive exponentials, so the upward $a_+$ and downward $a_-$ have equal moduli at opposite detunings, including their resonant limits. This proves (c). [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]
